title: Is it worth bringing your packshot photo production in-house?
h1: Before setting up an e-commerce photo studio: the questions to ask
metaTitle: Insourcing your product photos: 7 questions before investing
description: Volumes, time per product, difficult products, provider or in-house studio, full cost of an image: seven questions to decide whether to bring your product photography in-house.
author: PackshotCreator
content:
Article updated on October 14, 2026.

An in-house photo studio is rarely justified by how beautiful an image looks. It is justified by a flow: how many products arrive, how many views each one needs, where the time is lost between a sample arriving and going live, and what will still be left to outsource.

Here are the seven questions to settle before investing, in the order they come up. They point to no particular piece of equipment or brand: your answers form the specification for your future studio, or the proof that you do not need one.

Series · Producing your product images

  1. 1Decide Before setting up an e-commerce photo studio: the questions to ask
  2. 2Produce E-commerce photo studio: organizing reliable image production

Why do you want to produce your images in-house?

In brief

Because a specific need demands it: a short time to go live, products that arrive continuously, items that must not leave your premises, or consistency to maintain from one season to the next. “Saving money” is not enough of a reason on its own: it has to be checked with a full calculation (see the question “How do you estimate the full cost of producing an image?”).

PackshotCreator sums up the split of roles like this:

“A photographer or an external studio produces polished images, particularly for campaigns and editorial series. In-house production is mostly justified when items arrive continuously and need to go online quickly.”

PackshotCreator, “Packshot mode” page, 01/10/2026

Four reasons hold up against a calculation:

  • Pace. New arrivals, restocks, colors added mid-season: in-house, a product is photographed as soon as it arrives, without waiting for a shoot slot.
  • Lead time. Every day between a product’s receipt and its going live is a day its listing stays without an image, or with an incomplete one.
  • Sensitive items. Samples, prototypes, one-of-a-kind or confidential pieces before a launch stay on your premises.
  • Consistency. The shooting templates stay in the company: the next collection is photographed under the same conditions, even if the operator changes.
What to check

Write your reason in a single sentence, then pair it with an indicator you can measure today:

  • the time between a sample’s receipt and its image going online;
  • the number of products waiting for images;
  • the share of images redone each year: restocks, new colors, changed packaging;
  • visible differences in look across a category page.

Without a starting value, you will not know whether the studio kept its promise.

How many SKUs and views do you actually need to produce?

In brief

Count in images, not in products: SKUs × variants actually photographed × views per product, plus restocks, new colors and reshoots. It is this total, spread over the year and across the busy weeks, that sizes a studio.

Two parameters weigh as much as annual volume: how regularly products arrive and the share of images to be redone. A stable catalog does not call for the same studio as a collection renewed every season and delivered within a few weeks. PackshotCreator writes this about fashion collections:

“When SKUs and colors number in the hundreds, redoing the settings for every session takes time and multiplies the risk of inconsistencies between images.”

PackshotCreator, “Packshot mode” page, 01/10/2026

There is no universal threshold. For one specific piece of equipment, a studio that photographs and measures products in a single cycle, Sébastien Jourdan places profitability at “not below a thousand products a year, according to Orbitvu” (“Alphashot XL G2: product photos, dimensions, weight and data in a single cycle”, 14/07/2026). This benchmark applies to that type of equipment, not to every studio: work out your own figures with your own data.

See the method in practice

Fill in these five lines before requesting any quote:

Catalog to redo
SKUs × variants × views. Source: your PIM or your ERP.
New arrivals this year
Same calculation. Source: the collection or purchasing plan.
Images to redo
Restocks, colors and changed packaging. Source: the request history.
Reshoots
Images redone after validation. Source: reshoot tracking, if there is any.
Peak activity
The busiest week of the year. Source: the sales calendar.

Then divide the annual total by the number of actual production days, and compare with the peak: a studio sized on the average overflows during the busy weeks.

Where does the time go between a product’s arrival and its published image?

In brief

Rarely in the shooting itself. Pressing the shutter takes less than a second; the time goes into preparing the product, adjusting the settings, clipping paths, preparing the files, and every handoff from one person to the next.

Sébastien Jourdan’s experience

“Taking a photo takes less than a second. What lengthens the production of a packshot is mostly the work around it: preparing the product, repositioning it, adapting the lighting, then processing the images and preparing the files.”

Sébastien Jourdan, photographer and president of Sysnext (PackshotCreator), field benchmarks published on the e-commerce packshot page, 28/09/2026

After capture, the work goes on. According to the same field benchmarks, “clipping and file preparation can still take two to three times as long as the shooting itself. Images also have to be named, margins adjusted, and the dimensions required by each sales channel produced.”

Handoffs cost time too. About a chain where photography, measurement and data entry take place at three workstations, Sébastien Jourdan writes: “Three workstations. Three manual handlings. At every handoff, a chance to make a mistake, and time lost.”

See the method in practice

Time about ten representative products, including the hardest ones, at each step:

Preparation
Unpacking, cleaning, steaming out wrinkles, shaping, positioning. Pitfall: forgetting the time spent finding the sample.
Settings
Choosing or adjusting the lighting and the camera. Pitfall: counting them once, when they come back with every new product family.
Shooting
All the views planned for a product. Pitfall: confusing photos with products.
Processing
Clipping, retouching, cropping, checking. Pitfall: counting only the visible retouching.
Files
Naming, variants, export, verification. Pitfall: forgetting it because someone else handles it.

Then calculate capacity: if a day has H truly productive hours and a product takes t minutes, all steps included, capacity is roughly 60 × H ÷ t products per day. Fictional example: 6 productive hours and 12 minutes per product give 30 products per day.

Order of magnitude published by PackshotCreator: “a well-organized production can reach 200 to 300 photos taken and finalized per day with an automated studio”, whereas in a studio where these operations are carried out separately, “exceeding 50 photos a day, processing included, often remains difficult”. These field benchmarks “vary depending on the products, how they are prepared and the views required”: they give an order of magnitude, and your own measurement remains the reference.

Which products are likely to give your future studio trouble?

In brief

Those that reflect light, let it through, change appearance depending on the angle, are very small or very bulky, or whose color is hard to reproduce. List them before choosing equipment: they are what sizes it, not your easy products.

Sébastien Jourdan’s experience

About the products that come up most often in demonstrations:

“A reflection on a steel watch. A transparent bottle that disappears into the white background.”

Sébastien Jourdan, “Migrating an old PackshotCreator studio to Orbitvu and its AI”, 25/09/2026

The angle matters as much as the material. On the e-commerce packshot page, the example given is a watch: “perfectly lit from the front”, in a three-quarter view and with no change of lighting it can show “a reflection” on the dial that “hides the details you wanted to show”.

  • Shiny surfacespolished metal, watch crystal, lacquer, varnish

    Reflections change with the angle.

    Plan for: one lighting setup per view.

  • Transparent productsglass, bottles, packaging

    The outline can blend into the white background.

    Plan for: a dedicated background and lighting, and a check of the clipping.

  • Small objectsjewelry, technical parts

    The product’s entire depth must be sharp.

    Plan for: focus stacking.

  • Bulky productsfurniture, bicycles, equipment

    Size of the booth or turntable, load, handling.

    Plan for: the dimensions and weight of your largest products.

  • Soft materialstextiles, soft leather goods

    Shaping can take longer than shooting.

    Plan for: supports, padding, preparation time.

  • Difficult colorsblacks, whites, saturated colors

    A poorly reproduced color is discovered when the parcel is opened.

    Plan for: an on-screen comparison with the product.

For materials, PackshotCreator keeps to a simple rule: “each family of materials deserves its own lighting template, tested on a representative piece” (“Packshot mode” page, 01/10/2026).

What to check
  • the share of each difficult family in your catalog;
  • the most troublesome product in each family, to keep for the test (see the question “Which products should you absolutely test before investing?”);
  • the dimensions and weight of your largest products;
  • rendering requirements: reflections accepted or not, drop shadow, background.

Should you produce everything in-house or keep external providers?

In brief

Rarely one or the other entirely. Packshots from the regular flow suit in-house production; campaigns, lookbooks, outdoor shoots and elaborate staging can stay with a photographer or a studio. The decision is made by type of image, not as a block.

To explore this choice further, Sébastien Jourdan’s view on the decision to bring production in-house extends this analysis.

“Campaigns, lookbooks, outdoor shoots or elaborate staging: these one-off productions can remain entrusted to a photographer or a studio. A mixed organization is possible: catalog packshots in-house, campaigns outside.”

PackshotCreator, “Packshot mode” page, 01/10/2026
Decision grid, to be filled in for each type of image
CriterionBetter in-houseBetter with a provider
Arrival paceContinuous, in small batchesIn campaigns, on planned dates
Time to go liveShort: a few days at mostCompatible with an external schedule and the shipping of samples
Nature of the imagesRepeatable packshots, same angles from one season to the nextCampaigns, staging, outdoors
One-of-a-kind or confidential itemsStay on your premisesHave to travel, under conditions
Consistency over timeShooting templates kept within the companyDepends on written guidelines and how closely they are followed
SkillsTo be trained: “according to Orbitvu, basic training is enough for routine packshots, with no prior photography experience”Provided by the provider
If you keep a provider

Write a delivery specification, which will also be valid for your future in-house studio:

  • the file naming convention;
  • the expected views and their order;
  • the delivery dimensions and formats, per channel;
  • the background, margins and shadow;
  • the right to reuse the images on all your channels;
  • the lead time and the validation process.

Also read which type of studio for your in-house shoots

How do you estimate the full cost of producing an image?

In brief

Add up everything that happens between a sample’s arrival and the image going online, then divide by the number of images actually published. The price of a shoot says almost nothing about the cost of a published image.

Comparing a provider’s quote with the price of equipment means comparing two different pieces of the same cost. List the cost items on both sides:

In-house

  • the equipment and its depreciation;
  • the space: shooting, receiving, storage of samples;
  • the time of each step, measured in the question “Where does the time go”;
  • training and skills development;
  • maintenance and software;
  • reshoots.

With a provider

  • the shoots and retouching invoiced;
  • the shipping and tracking of samples;
  • coordination and validations;
  • the wait before going live;
  • reshoots and add-ons;
  • file preparation per channel, if it is not included.

Full cost of an image = (the year’s fixed costs + variable costs) ÷ images published during the year.

PackshotCreator’s return-on-investment calculator follows this same framework with your own figures. It does not replace measuring your actual times.

What to check

Lead time has a cost, even if it appears on no invoice: a product waiting for an image is not on sale online, or is on sale with an incomplete listing. Put a figure on it separately, with the sales team, rather than ignoring it.

Compare at equal volume: the cost per image of an in-house studio falls as volume rises, whereas per-image billing does not.

Which products should you absolutely test before investing?

In brief

Your five most difficult products to photograph, not the easiest ones. A test on simple products tells you nothing about the cases that will cost you time, nor about the fidelity of the images on your difficult materials.

Sébastien Jourdan puts it this way: “choose five products, the most difficult to photograph in your range” (“Migrating an old PackshotCreator studio to Orbitvu and its AI”, 25/09/2026). Bring them along with the list of expected views and a sample of a file published on one of your channels, so you can judge the result under real conditions.

During the test, observe:

  • the actual time per product, from setup to export, all views included;
  • the number of manual interventions after capture;
  • how reflections, transparencies and colors render, compared with the product placed next to the screen;
  • the exported files: name, dimensions, margins, background, in line with your channels;
  • reproducibility: redo one of the products with the saved setting, and compare the two images.
See the method in practice

For each product tested, note five criteria: time, retouching, fidelity, files, reproducibility. Three levels are enough: compliant, to be redone, blocking.

A blocking criterion on a family that carries weight in your catalog is a reason to reconsider the equipment you have in mind, or to keep that family with a provider.

Checklist before investing

The need

  • The reason for going in-house fits in a single sentence and rests on an indicator measured today.

The volumes

  • The number of images to produce per year is calculated: SKUs × variants × views, plus restocks and reshoots.
  • The busiest week of the year is identified.

The time

  • The time per product is measured on about ten representative products, step by step.
  • The required capacity is expressed in products per day.

The products

  • The difficult families are listed, with the most troublesome product of each.
  • The dimensions and weight of the largest products are recorded.

The organization

  • What stays with a provider is decided, with a delivery specification.

The cost

  • The full cost of a published image is calculated for in-house production and for the provider.

The test

  • Five of the most difficult products have been tested, exported files included.
  • One product was redone with the saved setting, and the two images compared.

Decision made? Article 2 of the series is about production: E-commerce photo studio: organizing reliable image production.
